extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and instructors in transition-to-proof / discrete mathematics courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing clear, correct, undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (transition-to-proof course style). Emphasizes identifying logical form, following templates, complete English sentences, variable discipline, and explicit conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always state what you are proving
rubrics_metrics.description: State at the start what you are proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin a proof by clearly announcing the proposition or claim you will prove so the reader knows the goal and logical form to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always state what you have proved
rubrics_metrics.description: State at the end what you have proved (Q.E.D., □).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude with an explicit statement that the desired result has been achieved (e.g., 'Thus, ...', 'Therefore, ...', or the box/Q.E.D.) to signal completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complete English sentences with mathematical symbols inside them, never instead of them
rubrics_metrics.description: Write each proof step as a complete English sentence, embedding mathematical symbols within sentences rather than replacing prose with formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain readable paragraphs; avoid chains of standalone symbols. This improves clarity and makes logical connections explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin sentences with a mathematical symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce context or a subject word before symbols so sentences read grammatically and clearly (e.g., 'Let x be ...' rather than starting with 'x ∈ ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'let' to introduce new variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new variables with 'let' (e.g., 'Let n be an integer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State variable type and scope at introduction to avoid ambiguity and misuse later in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'thus', 'therefore', 'hence' to mark logical conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use phrases such as 'thus', 'therefore', or 'hence' to signal logical consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly mark inferential steps so the reader can follow the deduction. Reserve such words for genuine conclusions, not mere restatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: One method per proof when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to use a single proof method rather than mixing multiple techniques within the same proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the most direct, appropriate method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction, etc.) and avoid 'scaffolding' from other methods leaking into the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'if … then' (implication) from 'iff' (equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to treat implication and equivalence differently; don't conflate 'if ... then' with 'iff'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving iff statements, explicitly handle both directions, and label them if helpful ('Proof of ⇒', 'Proof of ⇐').

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing converse with contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid confusing the converse of an implication with its contrapositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that proving the converse is not the same as proving the contrapositive; only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using 'any' ambiguously
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the word 'any' in an ambiguous way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about quantification—distinguish 'for all', 'there exists', and the intended scope of 'any' to prevent logical ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgetting one direction of an iff
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving an 'iff' statement, do not forget to prove both directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly structure the proof to show both 'if' and 'only if' parts; failing to do so renders the argument incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing the proof of the converse and calling it the proof of the implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present a proof of the converse and claim it proves the original implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the direction proven matches the stated implication; label direction to avoid this common error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misnaming the proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not name the wrong proof method (e.g., claim 'proof by contradiction' when no contradiction is reached).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either correctly identify the method used or omit naming it; if you claim a method, ensure the structure of the proof corresponds to that method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables introduced inside one case carried into another
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using variables introduced inside one case in a different case where they have not been defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly scope variables within cases; reintroduce or redefine them when moving between cases to prevent invalid reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction proofs without explicit base case
rubrics_metrics.description: Always include an explicit base case when using induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and verify the base case before the inductive step; omission makes the inductive argument incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs without verification of the witness
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving existence, verify that the candidate witness actually satisfies the required property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concrete witness or constructive argument and show it meets the conditions, rather than merely asserting existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-equality proofs that show only one inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim set equality after proving only one direction of inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove A = B, show both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A; prove and label each inclusion explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof templates matching logical form (∀, ∃, ⇒, ⇔, ¬, ∧, ∨)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each logical form, start with Hammack's (Velleman-echoed) starting template and finish with the corresponding completion template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the logical form of the statement (universal, existential, implication, equivalence, negation, conjunction, disjunction) and follow the matching template, writing the argument in well-formed English paragraphs rather than isolated symbolic steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the logical form of the statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and state the logical form (e.g., ∀, ∃, implication, iff) of the proposition you are proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification informs which template and structure the proof should follow and helps the reader anticipate the argument's flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: The matching proof template is followed
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the appropriate proof template for the identified logical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the starting and completion templates provided for that logical form so the argument is organized and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variables are introduced before use, with type stated
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce all variables before using them, and state their type (e.g., 'Let n be an integer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear introductions prevent ambiguity and scope errors; state domains, ranges, or other typing information as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each step is in a complete English sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every step of the proof should be written as a full English sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid terse symbolic chains; sentences should embed mathematical notation to make logical connections explicit and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The conclusion is explicit (□ or 'as required')
rubrics_metrics.description: End with an explicit concluding statement that the result has been achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a closing sentence such as 'Therefore, ...', 'Hence, ...', or the Q.E.D. box to mark completion so graders/readers know the argument is finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only the necessary technique is used; no scaffolding from other methods leaks in
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should use the most appropriate technique and avoid unnecessary use of other methods that clutter the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the proof focused and avoid mixing methods (e.g., avoid a direct proof that secretly uses contradiction without stating it).

rubrics_metrics.name: The reader can verify the proof line-by-line without filling in unstated steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs with enough detail so a reader can follow each step without having to supply omitted justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not every trivial algebraic manipulation needs elaboration, do not skip key logical transitions; include intermediate steps where the inference is not obvious.
